item.text: {"text":"Research supports controlling negative reliability alongside hardness. [SimDCL (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112257) addresses sequential contrastive sampling bias through false-positive/negative filtering. [Curricular weighting (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2024.120534) introduces negatives from easy to hard and regularizes their weights to reduce false-negative influence; this is general contrastive-learning evidence, not a NextItNet result. [Sampled-softmax analysis (2024)](https://zlstwebsite.github.io/Zlst/publication/on-the-effectiveness-of-sampled-softmax-loss-for-item-recommendation/) shows that the objective already emphasizes hard negatives through informative gradients. Thus, explicitly selecting only the highest-scoring negatives can compound hardness. A [sequential-recommendation sampling study (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds dataset-dependent accuracy/popularity trade-offs, arguing against a universally optimal sampler.\n\nPractical hypothesis for this task: retain one NextItNet per category, warm up with uniform sampled-softmax candidates, then gradually introduce a modest fraction of semi-hard candidates scored by that same network. Exclude padding, the positive target, duplicate candidates, and known training-history positives; retain uniform candidates to preserve coverage. Cap or smoothly reduce contributions from extremely hard candidates rather than declaring them additional positives: high model scores alone cannot establish relevance. Treat these choices as experimental adaptations, not a published recipe or guaranteed debiasing. Compare uniform sampled softmax, curriculum sampling, and capped negative weighting at matched candidate counts using macro validation HR@10. Electronics’ supplied 6.84% wrong-rank rate motivates testing discrimination, but does not measure false-negative prevalence. No teacher, separately fitted scorer, or inference fusion is required."}
